en_summary: Random thoughts on Jensen: met wife Lori at 17, started Nvidia at 30, spent 33 years building it into one of the most important companies. Suggests he missed youth experiences especially dating, and human nature may drive wanting those even at 60 with success. Not justifying the reckless actions that cost him the company he built from scratch, with Nvidia logo tattooed, called it his life's work. Saddest part is how quickly he was pushed out.
text:
Some random thoughts about Jensen.

Jensen met his wife Lori when he was just 17, got married, had kids, and started Nvidia at 30.

He then spent the next 33 years working his ass off building Nvidia into one of the most important companies in the world.

I imagine he probably missed out on a lot of things most young people experience, especially dating and relationships.

I think it’s just human nature. When you’re young and don’t get to experience certain things, you may feel like you’re missing out. And sometimes that feeling stays with you for the rest of your life.

Even when you’re 60, with all the money and success in the world, you may still want to experience what you missed in your 20s.

Maybe that’s part of what happened to Jensen. I don’t know.

I’m not trying to justify what he did. He was incredibly reckless, and it cost him something he spent more than half his life building.

But I also think we sometimes forget that Jensen is just a human being, with desires and weaknesses like the rest of us.

Maybe he spent so much of his life building Nvidia that somewhere along the way, he wanted to experience the life he never really had.

The saddest part for me is how quickly he was pushed out of the very company he built from scratch.

This is a man who literally has the Nvidia logo tattooed on his body, who has called Nvidia his life’s work, working every waking hour, and who dedicated more than half his life to it.

text:
$CBRS — the guide did the heavy lifting.

$CBRS builds wafer-scale AI chips — one giant chip instead of many small ones — and increasingly sells access to them as a cloud service rather than selling the hardware. Customers rent inference capacity, $CBRS keeps the chips and charges for use. That shift is the story: cloud revenue is growing fast while hardware sales shrink.

Today's print split in two. On the headline numbers it missed, with a wider loss. On its own core measure it beat, with core revenue of $230.9M. Then the guide did the work: next quarter is guided at $310–330M of core revenue, well above consensus, against a $26B backlog, and a new agreement with $MSFT was disclosed, size undisclosed. Shares jumped after hours.

The honest distinction: a raised guide and a big backlog prove demand is real. They do not prove profitability is near — the loss widened a lot on the headline numbers, and the gap between the core measure and the headline is wide. The reliability question from the short seller was answered by the CEO weeks ago; what this print tested was whether the economics hold up, and the cloud growth is the evidence for it.

Long term, if the cloud model scales, $CBRS becomes a recurring-revenue inference provider with a cost edge from building at wafer scale. If hardware economics or chip reliability bite, the story is the capex. The print backs the demand side. The cost side is still being proven.

$NBIS — the print beat, the funding plan didn't.

$NBIS rents out AI compute. It builds data centers full of GPUs and sells the capacity to customers training and running AI models, on multi-year contracts. The model is contract-first: customers sign long deals and pay upfront, and $NBIS uses that money to build the next data center.

The honest distinction: contracted revenue proves demand is real. It does not prove the build is funded. The offset is that customers are effectively financing the expansion — prepayments plus contract-backed financing are meant to cover most of next year's build. What that does not prove is that the pace holds if a customer slows down, or if debt markets stay shut to names like this.
Long term, if it executes, the contracted backlog converts into a very large revenue base. The risk is the gap between building now and getting paid later. That gap is the whole thesis now.

$MPLX has now increased its quarterly distribution by 12.5% for three consecutive years!

The Chowder Rule adds a stock’s dividend yield to its annual dividend growth rate to assess its combination of income and growth.

MPLX owns pipelines, storage terminals, natural-gas gathering and processing facilities, and infrastructure that separates natural gas liquids into usable products.

Customers primarily pay fees to move, store, and process energy products.

Long-term agreements with Marathon Petroleum include minimum-volume commitments and payments for reserved capacity-

Commodity prices still affect production activity and certain processing arrangements, but MPLX’s earnings are less directly dependent on the price of each barrel produced.

text:
You could get paid $1,230 today on 100 shares of $AMD you already own.

It's called a covered call, and here's how it works:

$AMD trades around $582, so 100 shares are worth about $58,200. You sell one $700 call expiring December 18 and collect about $12.30 a share, or $1,230, up front. That strike is about 20% above today's price.

In exchange, you agree to sell your 100 shares at $700 if AMD is above that price on December 18.

At expiration, one of two things happens:

1. $AMD finishes below $700. The call expires worthless. You keep the $1,230 and your shares, a 2.1% return in 36 days, and you're free to sell another call.

2. $AMD finishes above $700. Your shares are sold at $700. That's an $11,805 gain from today's price plus the $1,230 premium, or $13,035 in total (22.4%).

You don't have to wait until expiration either. I usually buy the call back once it has lost about half its value, then sell the next one.

The catch: your upside stops at $700. If $AMD runs to $800, the gains above $700 go to the call buyer. The premium also doesn't protect you much on the way down. It only cushions $12.30 a share, so your breakeven from today's price is $569.65.

$AMD isn't expected to report earnings again until after December 18, so there's no earnings report inside this trade.

Only sell a call at a strike where you'd be happy to sell your shares.

Not financial advice. I share these for education.
